title: Parveen Hooda Completes Redemption With Asian Games Boxing Gold
excerpt: Three years after a 22-month doping ban cost her a bronze medal and an Olympic dream, the Rohtak boxer beat Chinese Taipei's Chen Nien-chin 3-2 in the women's 65kg final, dedicating the gold to her father, who has battled throat cancer.
body:
• Parveen Hooda won the women's 65kg boxing gold at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, beating Chinese Taipei's Chen Nien-chin 3-2 on a split decision.
  • It caps a three-year comeback from a 22-month WADA ban for whereabouts failures that stripped her of her 2023 Asian Games bronze and cost her a Paris 2024 Olympic quota.
  • She dedicated the gold to her father Lakhpat, who has battled throat cancer, and said she drew on the Bhagavad Gita during her darkest phase: "Do karma, don't worry about the result."
  • Her next targets are the World Cup in April and the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

Parveen Hooda completed one of the most remarkable comebacks in Indian boxing on Friday, winning the women's 65kg gold at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya with a 3-2 split-decision victory over Chinese Taipei's Chen Nien-chin — and hugging the boxer she had just beaten as the verdict was announced.

It was India's second women's boxing gold of the Games, and the first Asian Games title of the 26-year-old's career. She won the opening round on all five judges' cards, lost the second to a Chen onslaught, and did enough in the third to take the bout.

The long road back

Three years ago, Parveen won bronze at the Hangzhou Asian Games. Then came a whereabouts failure ruling that drew a 22-month suspension, the disqualification of all her results between December 2022 and May 2024 — including that bronze — and the loss of the Paris 2024 Olympic quota she had already secured. Her return at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games earlier this year ended in a quarterfinal defeat, 2-3 to England's Sacha Hickey.

"When all that happened to me, I was mentally down. Everything was over. I had to start from zero. I was sad for a few days. Then I reset my mind," Parveen told reporters after the final, in comments carried by IANS.

"I told myself that if I don't train now and don't make a comeback, I will live in regret all my life. Because of a small mistake, so much happened. So I decided to take everything the other way around."

— Parveen Hooda, Asian Games boxing champion

The ban ended in May last year. Parveen won the 60kg BFI Cup gold, then beat World Championships silver medallist Aneta Rygielska at the World Boxing Cup in New Delhi. In Aichi-Nagoya she dispatched 2025 World Championships silver medallist Navbakhor Khamidova 5-0 and China's Li Shu 5-0 in the semifinal.

She has also climbed from 57kg to 65kg in three years; coach Anil Malik said the camp focused on turning her strength into clear, scoring punches while improving footwork to evade heavier blows.

A promise to her father

The gold fulfilled a promise to her father Lakhpat, who has battled cancer for years — her mother Neelam Devi said he was diagnosed with stage-3 throat cancer and was still undergoing chemotherapy when the suspension hit in 2024 — and who is also a heart patient. Her mother sells buffalo milk to keep the household running. An assistant sub-inspector with the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, Parveen is the family's principal breadwinner, funding her father's treatment with her boxing earnings.

"When I went to the 2023 Asian Games in China, my father was hospitalized," she said. She kept that bronze medal on the wall at home as a reminder: "I kept the medal in the middle of the wall so every time I see it, I think I'm going to change its color and bring gold."

Strength from the Gita

Parveen also revealed that she drew strength from the Bhagavad Gita during the hardest phase of her career. "I was thinking about the result that is written in the Gita, which is 'Do karma, don't worry about the result,'" she said.

After the quarterfinal loss in Glasgow, she recalled standing in tears watching fellow Indian boxers succeed — then getting up the next morning for weight training. "I thought, what's the point of crying now? Let's do hard work. Otherwise, I will cry again in the next competition."

What's next

Her father told ANI that the next targets are the World Cup in April and the 2028 Olympics, and that villagers are planning a grand welcome home. Parveen said she would take time with her family before beginning preparations, with the World Championships next year the first step toward Los Angeles.

For Indian fans — including the diaspora that has followed every bout of the comeback — her arc is a familiar portrait of India's sporting pipeline: a working-class Haryana family, a daughter funding her father's cancer treatment through her sport, and a bronze medal kept on a wall until it could be turned into gold.
